tac.title: The Anti-Aging Centre
tac.heading: Making complex care feel clear.
tac.lead: A research-led digital experience that brings clarity, reassurance, and a consistent visual language to healthcare decisions.
tac.body:
01 / Context & role

Support a considered healthcare decision.

The Anti-Aging Centre needed a digital experience that explained its services while communicating reassurance and credibility. My agency role connected brand strategy, research synthesis, landing-page design, and the consultation flow. I worked with brand stakeholders and frontend developers, using Figma, wireframing, and component systems.

02 / Research synthesis

Understand the questions behind the first click.

The research explored how people seek information, compare options, and decide whether to contact a centre. Treatment effectiveness, safety and side effects, cost and accessibility, reputation, and personalized care were central considerations. This decision journey informed what information the landing pages needed to make visible before asking visitors to take action.

03 / Audience & messaging

Different motivations need different emphasis.

The project focused on adults aged 30–60, with two audience segments: ages 30–45 seeking proactive approaches, and ages 45–60 interested in rejuvenation. The design response used segmented messaging within repeatable landing-page templates. This allowed the emphasis to change while preserving a familiar structure.

04 / Handwritten ideation

Connect the brand’s character to interface choices.

Early handwritten notes explored the brand’s message, emotional tone, and essential characteristics. Clarity, consistency, credibility, and audience focus became useful criteria for later visual decisions. These notes are original project artifacts that show the thinking before the polished interface.

05 / Wireframes & user flow

Build a path from introduction to consultation.

The initial click-through landing pages provided a concise introduction before directing visitors onward. The sales landing page then developed into clearly defined sections: banner, why, understanding, benefits, science, client stories, and consultation. This sequence gives each section a role in the visitor’s decision process.

06 / Interaction details

Use consistent calls to action.

Button explorations tested treatments on light and dark backgrounds, including filled and outlined directions. A shared CTA style helped connect the different landing pages. The design documentation also defines button sizing and typography, making the intended treatment easier to reproduce across layouts.

07 / Visual design & content

Balance warmth with authority.

Muted colors, calm imagery, and structured layouts formed the visual direction. Modular content blocks and simplified terminology made complex service information more approachable. Scalable page variants allowed messaging to adapt to audience needs while retaining visual continuity.

Outcome / What changed

From complex service information to a structured consultation path.

Research synthesis shaped a clear sequence from service introduction and treatment information to consultation. Modular landing-page templates let the team adapt messaging for different audiences without redesigning the page structure. Consistent CTAs and documented visual components created a repeatable interface system. The supplied project documents these delivered changes; post-launch conversion and task-completion figures are not available.

abpal.title: ABPAL
abpal.heading: Clarity for a complex product world.
abpal.lead: Organizing an extensive electrical-products catalogue into an intuitive, production-ready web experience.
abpal.body:
01 / Project overview

A technical catalog needs a clear way in.

A B Pal Electricals (P) Limited is an electrical solutions provider in India specializing in the safe and dependable transmission of electric power. Its wide range of technical products called for a structured digital presence that would make exploration intuitive while reinforcing credibility and trust.

Working within a design agency, I led the UX and interface design process from stakeholder discovery through high-fidelity prototypes and production-ready interface specifications. I collaborated with brand stakeholders and frontend developers to connect the business requirements with a practical web experience.

02 / Stakeholder discovery

Translate business complexity into visitor priorities.

Regular stakeholder meetings helped clarify the product range, business requirements, and information visitors needed to explore the offering. These discussions translated dense business language and technical specifications into structured user flows and digestible content hierarchies.

  • Core product verticals
  • Business priorities
  • Key conversion goals
  • Target audience
  • Content depth requirements
The insight that shaped the direction

Credibility and clarity mattered more than visual experimentation. The experience needed to help visitors find information efficiently and trust what they were seeing.

03 / Information architecture

Help people recognize the right category.

The central information challenge was making an extensive product range manageable. A structured taxonomy grouped related offerings, while modular layouts gave each category a predictable presentation. Clear category entry points helped visitors move from the homepage into product exploration.

04 / Wireframing & user touchpoints

Resolve structure before adding visual detail.

I created low-fidelity wireframes to work through navigation depth, category structures, and content priority. Mapping the path from the homepage to product exploration helped identify how page sections and entry points should connect before the interface was developed in detail.

The wireframes established the content structure for the high-fidelity design, keeping attention on a clear route through the product information.

05 / Interface design

Make dense information easier to scan.

A restrained visual language supported the credibility of a technical business. Consistent interface standards, clear hierarchy, and modular content layouts organized product information into a professional, readable experience.

The design balances business identity with practical use: recognizable product categories, repeatable page patterns, and clear calls to action support exploration without unnecessary visual complexity.

06 / Design system

Build reusable parts for a growing product range.

I developed a component-based interface system in Figma to support consistency across the website. Reusable navigation, controls, and page elements provided a shared foundation for the product range and its responsive layouts.

Documented interface components and color choices helped connect the high-fidelity prototypes with production-ready specifications for the development team.

07 / Delivery & collaboration

Carry the design through to implementation.

Continuous collaboration with stakeholders and frontend developers helped align the design with real-world implementation constraints. The delivery focused on responsive behavior, consistent interface standards, and performance-aware UI implementation.

The live website brings the structured navigation, modular layouts, and component system together in a production experience.

08 / Challenges & solutions

Turn constraints into a clearer experience.

Dense product information

Response: A structured taxonomy and modular layouts make the extensive range easier to organize and navigate.

Trust in a technical domain

Response: Restrained visual styling and consistent interface standards reinforce the brand’s professional character.

Real-world delivery constraints

Response: Ongoing stakeholder and developer collaboration keeps the interface aligned with implementation needs.

Outcome / What changed

A product-heavy business became a navigable digital experience.

The final solution brings an extensive product range into a structured, professional website. The delivered experience combines:

  • Structured navigation across extensive product categories.
  • A clear, professional interface suited to a technical business.
  • Responsive behavior across devices.
  • A scalable component system for consistent page design.
  • Performance-aware implementation developed in collaboration with the frontend team.

Results across my work

Reported results include a 56% improvement in usability and task completion, along with increased site engagement.

khushi.title: Khushi Bafna
khushi.heading: Putting the photographer’s work first.
khushi.lead: A minimal photography portfolio shaped by the needs of the creator, design aspirants, and recruiters.
khushi.body:
The overview

Khushi Bafna

The goal was to create an easy-to-use portfolio for a photography enthusiast, giving her work a clear, curated presentation while supporting professional opportunities and creative inspiration.

01 / Research

Listening to both creator and audience

Client walkthroughs helped clarify the photographer’s perspective. Interviews with a head of department and a design aspirant added recruiter and viewer perspectives, alongside a review of existing photography portfolios.

02 / Synthesis

Understanding what viewers need

Personas, empathy maps, and an as-is scenario brought together different expectations. The research considered how visitors discover work, understand the creator, and navigate the portfolio.

03 / Structure

A simple path through the work

A user journey and wireframes organized the portfolio around accessible navigation and content. The visual direction used a minimal interface so the photographs could carry the experience.

Outcome & reflection

What the work delivered

A research-informed portfolio concept with user journeys and wireframes focused on content discovery and a simple viewing experience.
khushi.facts:
My roleUX/UI Designer
ScopeResearch, personas, empathy mapping, journeys, wireframes
Tools & methodsInterviews, comparative research, prototyping

rajasthan.title: Rajasthan Tourism
rajasthan.heading: Where heritage meets horizon.
rajasthan.lead: A visual identity that brings together Rajasthan’s sun, forts, and golden dunes.
rajasthan.body:
01 / The brief

A place, expressed through an identity.

This tourism identity brings Rajasthan’s architecture, warm landscape, and cultural character into one visual system. The aim was to create a recognizable mark that could travel consistently between a brand book, stationery, and visitor-facing objects.

02 / Sketching & exploration

Starting with pencil, shape, and place.

The original sketches explore ways to combine architectural silhouettes, the sun, desert forms, and lettering. Seeing the alternatives together reveals the move from individual regional cues toward a compact, unified symbol.

03 / The final direction

Four elements. One visual story.

The final logo brings together the sun, forts, desert, and Rajasthan logotype. The architectural forms reference historic forts; the sun and desert connect the identity to the region’s warm climate and golden dunes. The composition carries these references into a single recognizable mark.

04 / Building the system

Guidelines that make the identity repeatable.

Warm reds, terracotta, orange, and sand tones form the palette, supported by black and white. The guidelines define typography, color use, size, clearspace, and treatments to avoid. Clearspace uses the x-height of the “n” in the logotype, giving the mark a consistent area to breathe.

05 / Across touchpoints

From the page to the objects people keep.

Letterheads and business cards extend the identity into everyday communication. Badges, mugs, and apparel show how the same mark and palette can retain their character across different sizes, materials, and contexts.

Outcome / What changed

One identity, ready to work across different touchpoints.

The project translated separate regional references into a unified logo and a documented visual system. Clearspace, typography, color, and usage rules made the identity repeatable across stationery and merchandise, with applications shown below. The result is a complete identity system; tourism awareness or visitor-impact figures were not measured in this project.
